literal adjective and adverb

also literally, in the literal sense, word for word, literal translation, literal meaning, literal sense, learn word for word

classical

Quint. 8.3.24: cum sint autem verba propria, ficta, trānslāta
Traupman 247

proprius, propria, proprium

literal, used in its own sense (of a word)

A word used in its proper sense is verbum proprium, against trānslātum, figurative. Literally is propriē: magis propriē nihil possum dīcere (Cic. Phil. 2.77, Lewis & Short); Pōniturne «arma» propriē an figūrātē?, is “arma” used literally or figuratively? (Traupman 239).

Other words

  • propriē — literally, in the proper sense

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 2.77; Gell. 9.1.8 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 239, 247; Cic. Off. 3.3.13: quod propriē vērēque dīcitur (Lewis & Short s.v. proprius); Traupman 340: propriē (opp. figūrātē)

  • ad verbum — word for word, literally

    also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 1.4: fābellae Latīnae ad verbum dē Graecīs expressae (Lewis & Short); Traupman 247; Cic. Fin. 1.2.4: fābellae Latīnae ad verbum dē Graecīs expressae (Lewis & Short s.v. verbum); Traupman 340

    Of a translation or a quotation that follows the words exactly; Cicero also says verbum prō verbō reddere (Opt. Gen. 14) and verbum ē verbō for a single word rendered exactly (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • cum sint autem verba propria, ficta, trānslāta, propriīs dignitātem dat antīquitās

    and since words are literal, coined or figurative, age gives dignity to the literal onesQuint. 8.3.24

  • Pōniturne «arma» propriē an figūrātē? — Figūrātē.

    Is “arma” used literally or figuratively? — Figuratively.Traupman 239

See also figurative, translate, word, mean.
